INLA-style posterior approximation for any log-posterior

Source: R/inla-vanilla.R
inla_vanilla.Rd

Approximates the posterior of a parameter vector from its log density alone, using the approximation pipeline of INLAvaan with no latent field and nothing model-specific. The pipeline has four stages:

  1. Joint Gaussian (Laplace). The posterior mode \(\vartheta^*\) and the inverse Hessian \(\Omega\) there give a Gaussian approximation \(N(\vartheta^*, \Omega)\) and the Laplace estimate of the log marginal likelihood.

  2. VB mean correction. The Gaussian is recentred at \(\tilde\vartheta = \vartheta^* + \hat\delta\), the mean that maximises its expected log-posterior, with the covariance unchanged.

  3. Skew-normal marginals. For each parameter, the log-posterior is scanned along the conditional mode path of the Gaussian, corrected for the changing volume of the other parameters, and fitted by a skew-normal \(SN(\hat\xi_j, \hat\omega_j, \hat\alpha_j)\).

  4. Gaussian copula draws. sampling() couples the skew-normal marginals through the correlations of \(\Omega\).

Usage

inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init,
  grad = NULL,
  ...,
  vb = TRUE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  control = list()
)

Arguments

logpost

A function logpost(theta, ...) returning the log-posterior density (up to a constant) at the named numeric vector theta, on the unconstrained scale. See the section on writing logpost.

init

A named numeric vector of starting values. Its length sets the number of parameters and its names label them; unnamed values are called theta[1], theta[2], ..., and a repeated name is numbered in the same way.

grad

Optional function grad(theta, ...) returning the gradient of logpost as a numeric vector. When NULL (the default), finite differences are used.

...

Further arguments passed to logpost and grad, such as the data. As in stats::optim() and stats::nlminb(), they come after the gradient, and the arguments after them (vb, verbose, control) must be given by their full names, so data arguments cannot partially match them.

vb

Logical. Apply the VB mean correction? Default TRUE. It enters the log marginal likelihood, and the skew-normal means are checked against it (see summary.inla_vanilla()).

verbose

Logical. Show progress? Default TRUE.

control

A list of tuning parameters; see the section on control.

Value

An object of class inla_vanilla, with methods for print(), summary(), plot() and sampling(). It is a list holding, among other things:

  • summary: the posterior summary table (mean, SD, quantiles, mode).

  • mode, cov: the Laplace mode and covariance.

  • mean_vb: the VB-corrected mean (the mode when vb = FALSE).

  • sn: the skew-normal parameters xi, omega and alpha per parameter.

  • logml: the log marginal likelihood.

Writing logpost

The approximation works on an unconstrained scale: every parameter must be free to take any real value. Reparameterise anything constrained, for example a standard deviation \(\sigma > 0\) as \(\log\sigma\), a probability as its logit, or a correlation as its Fisher \(z\). Means and regression coefficients need no change.

Return -Inf wherever the density is zero or cannot be evaluated, such as outside the support or where a matrix is not positive definite (NA and NaN count the same). The scans and the VB nodes reach several posterior SDs from the mode, and an error raised there stops the fit.

logpost is then the log density of the parameters you pass. When a prior is stated on the natural scale, include the log-Jacobian of the transformation: with \(\vartheta = \log\sigma\) and a prior \(p(\sigma)\), the prior term is \(\log p(e^\vartheta) + \vartheta\). Leaving it out targets a different posterior, not a worse approximation of the same one, and nothing downstream can detect it.

The choice of parameterisation also sets the quality of the approximation, since each parameter gets its own skew-normal on the scale you choose. Scales on which the posterior is close to Gaussian (log standard deviations, Fisher-\(z\) correlations, logits) work best. Natural-scale or derived quantities are available through sampling(fit, fun = ...).

The log marginal likelihood is an estimate of \(\log p(y)\) only when logpost returns the full \(\log p(y, \vartheta)\), including every normalising constant of the likelihood and the prior. Otherwise it is off by the missing constants.

Accuracy

The skew-normal marginals capture skewness that the Laplace approximation misses, and they are accurate to the extent that a skew-normal fits each marginal (see the diagnostics in summary.inla_vanilla()). Like INLAvaan, each marginal is scanned along a straight line through the mode, and the changing volume of the other parameters enters only to first order. When a parameter's spread depends strongly on another, poorly determined parameter, its marginal comes out too narrow, by a factor that vanishes as O(1/n). Examples are a regression coefficient or a mean when the noise SD is uncertain. For a normal mean with unknown variance the SD is about 11\ too small at n = 12, 3\

Gradients

grad is optional. Without it, derivatives come from finite differences of logpost, and the number of calls grows quickly with the number of parameters m. The mode and Hessian take about m^2 + 6m calls. The marginals take about m(n_grid + 2m + 5). The VB correction takes about (m + 1)(2m^2 + 1) calls per sweep, over a few sweeps, so it dominates beyond a handful of parameters: at m = 20 a fit makes on the order of 50,000 calls. With grad, the VB correction takes 2m^2 + 1 gradient calls per sweep instead, and the fit is faster and more accurate. For more than about 10 parameters, supply grad, or set vb = FALSE to skip the VB correction (and its term in the log marginal likelihood).

A supplied grad is checked against finite differences at init, and its Jacobian at the mode is checked for symmetry, with a warning if either check fails. Any R function works for logpost and grad, including compiled code (Rcpp, TMB, RTMB). For a TMB object, which minimises, pass function(x) -obj$fn(x) and function(x) -as.vector(obj$gr(x)), with init = obj$par; its repeated names (one per element of a parameter vector) are numbered, as beta[1], beta[2], and so on.

Control

control is a list with any of:

  • n_grid: number of grid points per skew-normal scan, spread over \(\pm 4\) posterior SDs (default 21).

  • log_threshold: grid points whose log-posterior falls more than this below the maximum are ignored in the skew-normal fit (default -6).

  • vb_maxit, vb_tol: iteration limit (default 25) and convergence tolerance in posterior SDs (default 1e-3) for the VB correction.

  • nlminb: a list of stats::nlminb() controls for the mode search. iter.max and eval.max default to 1000 and 2000.

References

Jamil, H. and Rue, H. (2026). Approximate Bayesian inference for structural equation models using integrated nested Laplace approximations. doi:10.48550/arXiv.2603.25690

Jamil, H. and Rue, H. (2026). Implementation and workflows for INLA-based approximate Bayesian structural equation modelling. doi:10.48550/arXiv.2604.00671

See also

sampling() for posterior draws and derived quantities, summary.inla_vanilla() for diagnostics.

Examples

# Normal data with unknown mean and standard deviation, on the scale
# (mu, log sigma)
set.seed(1)
y <- rnorm(30, mean = 5, sd = 2)

logpost <- function(theta, y) {
  mu <- theta[["mu"]]
  sigma <- exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  sum(dnorm(y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, 10, log = TRUE) + # prior on mu
    dexp(sigma, rate = 1, log = TRUE) + # prior on sigma ...
    theta[["log_sigma"]] # ... and its Jacobian
}

fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0), y = y)
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 10 iterations [5ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.24σ [2ms]
#> ✔ Fitted 2 skew-normal marginals [7ms]
fit
#> ── INLAvanilla ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 20ms ──
#> 2 parameters · skew-normal marginals · VB-corrected
#> 
#>             Mean     SD   2.5%    50%  97.5%   Mode
#> mu         5.159  0.327  4.517  5.159  5.800  5.159
#> log_sigma  0.616  0.129  0.377  0.610  0.885  0.599
#> 
#> Log marginal likelihood: -66.38

# The posterior of sigma itself, through the draws
sigma <- sampling(fit, fun = function(theta) exp(theta[["log_sigma"]]))
quantile(sigma, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>     2.5%      50%    97.5% 
#> 1.444354 1.832695 2.455869
